description: The one example the brief provides, end to end.
asr: ask aditya to review the sarvam kiwi service
formatted: Ask Aditya to review the Sarvam Kiwi service.
expected: Ask Aaditya to review the Sarvam Kivi service.
rationale: Two learned identities in one sentence. 'Kiwi' here sits beside 'Sarvam' and 'service', which is the context that makes it the product rather than the fruit.

description: HEADLINE CLAIM. 'adithya' was never observed by the system; only 'aditya' was ever corrected. A dictionary cannot do this.
rationale: The correction taught a phonetic identity, not a string. 'th' is an aspirated t in Indian romanisation, so adithya collapses to the same key as aditya.

description: A second never-observed spelling, aspirate on the d instead of the t.
rationale: dh and d collapse identically to d.

description: Both aspirate and doubled vowel, never observed.
rationale: aa collapses to a and th collapses to t; two independent rules composing.

description: Two adjacent identities, both wrong, in a single noun phrase.
asr: the sarwam kiwi service is slow today
formatted: The Sarwam Kiwi service is slow today.
expected: The Sarvam Kivi service is slow today.
rationale: w and v collapse. Kivi is supported by the adjacent Sarvam and service context terms.
The match is on the stem; the possessive suffix is reattached rather than swallowed.
'dictionary' is a Kivi context term, supporting the product reading.

description: Formatter title-cased an acronym; memory knows the real shape.
rationale: Canonical casing is part of the memory entry, not a formatting rule.

description: Interior vowel drift defeats the strict key; the loose consonant key must catch it.
rationale: vekariya and vakaria share the consonant skeleton vkr but not the strict skeleton.

description: The variant that was actually observed during learning.
rationale: Directly observed surface; the easy end of the same mechanism.

description: Doubled consonant instead of doubled vowel, never observed.
asr: the sarras model handles code mixing
formatted: The Sarras model handles code mixing.
expected: The Saaras model handles code mixing.
rationale: Repeat collapse makes saaras and sarras identical.

description: Final vowel drift on a learned name.
rationale: Terminal ay/oy drift is common in romanised names; the consonant skeleton holds.

description: Three identities in one sentence, all wrong.
asr: ask aditya whether sarwam shipped the kiwi build
formatted: Ask Aditya whether Sarwam shipped the Kiwi build.
expected: Ask Aaditya whether Sarvam shipped the Kivi build.
rationale: Independent spans must each be decided on their own evidence.
Position must not change the decision.

description: Trailing comma must not break the match.
rationale: Punctuation is stripped for matching and restored for output.

description: Source span casing pattern is preserved on rewrite.
rationale: An all-caps span stays all-caps. We replace the word, not the user's emphasis.

description: An explicit dictionary add is trusted immediately and does not wait for a second confirmation.
rationale: The user stating a word outright is stronger evidence than inferring it from an edit.

description: KNOWN HARD, EXPECTED TO FAIL. b/v confusion is real in Indian ASR (Bekariya for Vekariya) but we deliberately do not map b to v globally.
rationale: A global b<->v rule would collapse bat/vat, bet/vet and ban/van. We judged the false-positive cost higher than this miss, and report the miss rather than hiding it.
